My friend @harrisonjaime is one of the best leaders & did extraordinary work in building a multiracial coalition that opened many doors for people like me who, as an Indian American of Hindu faith, never had a shot in politics growing up. 

My friend @davidsirota is passionate about the party returning to our roots of fighting for the working class & standing against foreign wars.

If we can come together, which we will, we will build one of the greatest coalitions for progressive change since A. Philip Randolph and Bayard Rustin championed the Freedom budget.

Let's build a movement that can transform our nation.

That begins in November.

That is our duty and destiny.

quoted.text:
To what end, David? 

Congrats… you won your seat running against the “establishment.” Threw mud all over the party. Now what?

Can you pass a bill by yourself? Nope. 

Can you get your agenda through a Republican majority? Good luck. 

Want to win the White House? To get to 270, you’re going to need some of those same folks you keep shitting on.

Run your own race. Tell folks where you disagree. But there’s a difference between that and telling everybody the whole damn party is worthless.

If you win,  but other Democrats lose, who’s passing your agenda?! 

It is the collective that makes things happen in our government and not the individual.  You have to find a way to work with folks. 

Otherwise you’re slashing the tires on the same damn bus you need to get somewhere. Make it make sense.

Bottomline- save the fights for the primary.  Let’s all win in the general!

They deserve accountability and justice. I will not stop fighting until they get it.

Three years ago, families in southern Israel woke up on a holiday morning to sirens and gunfire. By nightfall, Hamas terrorists had murdered nearly 1,200 people and dragged 251 hostages into Gaza. It was the deadliest day for the Jewish community since the Holocaust. The pictures of that day still haunt me the same way they haunt so many in our community. For many families here in South Florida, October 7 doesn’t feel like three years ago. It feels like yesterday. 

As a proud Jewish American and the grandson of Holocaust survivors, I know remembrance is not enough. It takes the courage to confront antisemitism on the far right and the far left, and to call out anyone who tries to excuse terrorism. 

No one should be afraid to walk into a synagogue or send their kids to school because they are Jewish. I will keep standing with our Jewish neighbors, today and every day.

text:
Three years ago, Israel was the victim of a terrorist attack by Hamas that killed nearly 1,200 civilians. Innocent lives were snuffed out, families murdered in cold blood, women raped, young people targeted because of who they are and where they called home.

But the violence of that day did not end on October 8. Its violence was contagious, plunging the region into chaos and years of war that have taken a toll on many thousands of people — Palestinians and Israelis. Israeli civilians were held hostage in dark tunnels by Hamas for hundreds of days, while being subject to rape, torture and murder. Palestinian civilians lost their lives as whole neighborhoods were destroyed, and they continue to endure, unimaginable conditions in Gaza; Palestinians still suffer increased violence and displacement in the West Bank. Civilians in Israel still live in fear of another promised attack by Hamas terrorists, and civilians in Northern Israel or Lebanon worry about being collateral damage in the continuing struggle between Israel and Hezbollah.

After three years, the pathway to peace and a lasting two-state solution is farther out of reach and tattered, while extremist voices have flourished in the Middle East.

This anniversary should be a solemn moment to recommit to the goal of two sovereign states, and rebuilding the pathway to that future. Just as we pushed to bring hostages home and achieve a ceasefire, we must continue to push for expanded aid to rebuild Gaza, for an end to Hamas’ ability to threaten Israel, and for a lasting agreement to end this conflict and ensure that Israelis and Palestinians may live side by side in peace, security, dignity, and mutual recognition.

Today, three years after the October 7th terrorist attack, we mourn the thousands of innocent lives lost. We mourn for children who lost their parents, for parents who lost their children, and for the countless families still reeling from unimaginable loss. 

We also condemn the vile antisemitism that took hold across the country and world immediately following – at the precise moment we should have been most united.

I want to take a moment to remember those our Hudson Valley community lost that day.

Judih and Gadi Haggai were not combatants or soldiers, but a school teacher and a musician. Ariel and Kfir Bibas were not prisoners of war, but children, babies, ripped away from their home and taken hostage by Hamas terrorists. They would be 3 and 7 years old today. Instead, their memories are being honored by the Ariel and Kfir Bibas Playroom at the Chabad of Ulster County. 

Today, on the anniversary of the deadliest attack on the Jewish people since the Holocaust, I join the Hudson Valley and the entire world in remembering those we have lost. We must also recommit to fighting the rising scourge of antisemitism in all its forms, wherever and whenever we see it. Most of all, we must keep pushing relentlessly for a just and lasting peace.

We cannot become numb to this conflict – nor to the hate that has followed. Too much and too many have been lost already. 

May this horrific anniversary of suffering and grief strengthen our resolve for hope and peace.

text:
Three years ago today, Hamas terrorists launched a brutal, barbaric — most inhumane — attack on the people of Israel. Homes, Kibbutzim, and families were burned. Families torn apart. Unspeakable crimes committed against women, children, and seniors. More than 1,200 people were killed and 250 taken hostage, including American citizens.

The cruelty and brutality of this attack demanded universal, international condemnation and American support for our ally and friend Israel.

I have traveled to Israel several times since October 7th, to meet with grieving Israeli families and government leaders. I met twice with Prime Minister Netanyahu, urging him to pursue justice — a just war — not vengeance, to be a partner for peace.

Today, thanks to the tireless advocacy from the families and to American leadership, all the living hostages have been reunited with their loved ones. The dead have been returned to be buried with dignity. Around the world, Jewish people just celebrated their first Rosh Hashanah without any hostages held in Hamas’ custody. But the scars of October 7th run deep and are lasting. The families of those who were killed, and those who were taken, will carry that grief for the rest of their lives. We all will.

Meanwhile, the region remains in turmoil. Millions of Gazans are still displaced and vulnerable, struggling to find the food, water, medicine, and shelter they need to survive. More than 70,000 innocent Palestinian civilians have been killed and thousands more wounded, so many of them children. and Israeli violations of the ceasefire are alarmingly common. In the West Bank, Israeli settlers continue to encroach on Palestinian land, using violence to injure, kill, and drive out Palestinian families, jeopardizing any chance at peace.

We owe it to all those who died, on that day and in the devastating war since, to build a better future. 

My prayer, and my work as a member of Congress, remains focused on supporting these essential pillars of peace: disarming of Hamas, a durable ceasefire to enable the mass distribution of humanitarian aid to the people of Gaza; a safe and secure future for Israel as a democratic home for the Jewish people; self-determination and dignity for the Palestinian people to rebuild their lives and create a democratic, sovereign state of their own; and a commitment by leaders around the world to these principles, that we might truly end the cycle of violence. 

In this work, I am guided by the Jewish teaching of “Tikkun Olam”— the call to repair the world — and by the Scripture which tells us: blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called children of God.

Today, we remember the suffering of October 7th. Tomorrow, we must continue the work, with mercy and moral clarity, each doing our part to make peace.

October 7th is a deeply painful day for so many here in Los Angeles and around the world. Today, we remember the nearly 1,200 innocent lives murdered on the deadliest day for Jews since the Holocaust, as well as the dozens of hostages who died in Hamas captivity. We also remember the immense pain, suffering, and loss experienced by both Israelis and Palestinians in the war that followed, including the tragic deaths of 60,000 civilians in Gaza.

As the representative of one of the largest Jewish populations in the country, I’ve often heard from members of the community that the pain of this day is revisited every time they read about the rise in antisemitic attacks targeting Jewish houses of worship, businesses, and beloved community members. I will always stand firm against antisemitism and hate in all forms.

There can never be another October 7th, nor a repetition of the brutality and suffering that followed. As we reflect on the pain of the last three years, we must continue pushing for lasting peace in the region through a two-state solution that allows both Israelis and Palestinians to live with dignity, security, and freedom.

text:
Today marks three painful years past the October 7th terrorist attack on Israel, when Hamas murdered more than 1,200 men, women, and children and abducted 251 others into brutal captivity. My heart and thoughts are with the countless families who have suffered an unthinkable, unbearable grief that came with that terrible day and will stay with them forever.

The vile tide of antisemitism and islamophobia that arrived in the October 7th attack’s aftermath has been felt by innocents throughout our world, including far too many of our Jewish and Muslim neighbors across Brooklyn. In the name of all those we have lost, and all others we hope to save, we must continue to stand against hatred in all its forms. The work of building a future where our coexistence is accepted as a source of strength, and not seen as an excuse to divide, must go on.

We can create a world where all are welcome, and safe, and loved – but only if we try.

text:
Over the past week, I have been rewatching gut-wrenching videos taken by Hamas terrorists of their own massacre of Israeli families, grandparents and children three years ago today, reading about new accounts of hostages in brutal captivity, and thinking back to my own experience taking my young children back and forth to a bomb shelter as rockets rained down from Gaza. I think often about how the Iron Dome may very well have saved my family’s lives that day, along with thousands of other innocent civilians in Israel. 

Since 2007 when Israel withdrew from Gaza and turned control over to Hamas, neither Israel nor Gazan civilians have been in charge. Instead, it has been governed by a globally-designated terrorist group whose stated mission and sole focus is to wipe out Israel, which they tried to do three years ago and then carried on for years by holding hundreds of Israeli hostages in brutal conditions in their terror tunnel network. That terrorist group remains armed and dangerous in Gaza today, still fully committed to wiping out Israel, the world’s only safe haven for Jews and the only democracy in the region. 

If you are someone — like me — who wants peace in the region and self-determination for all people there, then Hamas represents a complete and total obstacle to that goal. As we remember the devastation inflicted by them on this day three years ago, we must also recognize that Iranian-backed terrorist groups such as Hamas remain an existential threat not only to peace in the region but also to democracy around the world. 

Today is a day of mourning and remembrance of all those innocent lives lost, those who were wounded both physically and mentally, the hostages who survived through unspeakable conditions, and a country shaken to its core by the genocidal attack three years ago. Tomorrow, I will continue working towards a path to peace, security and self-determination for Israelis and Palestinians alike.

Am Yisrael Chai.

text:
Border communities deserve a strong federal partner and investments that address the needs we see every day in South Texas.

In the FY26 Energy and Water Development Appropriations bill, I helped secure $5.5 million for the Southwest Border Regional Commission, a $500,000 increase over FY24.

We are already seeing what these investments mean back home. The Commission has provided $330,000 to help Webb County families in colonias access safe drinking water, $871,010 for a new Rural Emergency Clinic in Jim Hogg County, and $664,890 to support the revitalization of a historic building in downtown Laredo for small-business and economic-development programs. The Jim Hogg clinic will bring primary and urgent care, basic diagnostics, and telehealth closer to residents, while the Laredo project is designed to support downtown revitalization and local businesses. 

I helped get the Southwest Border Regional Commission off the ground because our border communities deserve access to the same federal resources as communities across the country. As a senior member of the House Appropriations Committee, I will continue working to make sure the Commission has the resources to invest in water, health care, infrastructure, and economic opportunity across South Texas.

When I toured the USS Lincoln, I arrived with a lot of questions. 321 days at sea. 200 of those days without a single stop at a port of call.

Undoubtably, there is truth to some of the stories and headlines; a ship with 5,000 souls aboard has that many stories and that many truths.

The real question is whether this war, which put the USS Lincoln at sea for so long, is a justified or necessary one. Whether the American people have authorized the deployment of our soldiers and sailors, airmen and marines in this way. Whether Congress, as the people’s proxy, has exercised our oversight and budgetary authority over this war and over the Department of Defense.

My answer to these questions is no.

What happened last night at Northwestern was unacceptable. It is disgraceful that the community cannot gather to honor October 7 survivors without fear and interruption. There must be an investigation into the incident and the perpetrators must be held accountable.

Imagine being so committed to a political narrative that you would rather silence survivors of October 7 than let them share the truth. And the fact that so many are openly celebrating October 7 on campuses and places across the country makes it even more grotesque.

This is exactly what Ahmed Fouad Alkhatib points to: a “pro-Palestine” movement so consumed by its own narrative that many of its loudest voices still cannot bring themselves to unequivocally condemn Hamas or acknowledge the horror of October 7.

You don't get to celebrate a terrorist group and then pretend you are standing for humanity. You don't get to chant about justice while trying to prevent survivors from being heard.

October 7 was not "liberation." It was not "resistance." It was a day in which Hamas murdered, kidnapped, and brutalized innocent civilians. Full stop.

quoted.text:
Three years after the catastrophic day Hamas unleashed on Israelis and on the Palestinian people in Gaza, the majority of the “pro-Palestine” industrial complex still refuses to utter a single word of condemnation or assign any responsibility to the Islamist terror group that destroyed the Gaza Strip and triggered the most calamitous chapter in modern Palestinian history.

Today alone, I have seen dozens of posters and announcements for rallies, protests, and a so-called “week of rage.” Endless groups across the Western world, including the United States, whether community-based, campus-based, nonprofit, or cultural, are celebrating and commemorating “three years of resistance and genocide.” In almost comical language, many declare October 7 as the beginning of genocide in Gaza while making no mention of the bloodshed, murder, beheadings, torture, mutilation, burning people alive, executions, sexual assault, and hostage taking that initiated the disaster which befell the Palestinian people.

It is as if Israeli and Jewish lives are invisible. As if civilians were not slaughtered in their homes while they slept. As if partygoers were not massacred. As if the attack was not entirely unprovoked while a ceasefire was in place between Israel and Hamas. It is a complete erasure of cause and effect and a refusal to grasp that choices and actions produce consequences.

I have yet to see a mainstream Arab, Palestinian, or Muslim American organization, let alone prominent “pro-Palestine” academics, journalists, community groups, or notable individuals, issue a statement acknowledging Hamas’s responsibility and culpability for the devastation inflicted on Gaza. Even within the imbalance of power and the overwhelming suffering caused by Israeli decisions, there is still ample space to acknowledge the humanity of Israeli victims and the injustice of what happened to them. More importantly, there is immense space to speak honestly about the horrendous damage caused to Palestinians by the Jihadi fascism of Hamas, which has devastated Gazans over the two decades of its rule.

Three years later, Israelis, Jews, and Zionists are commemorating the anniversary while engaging in introspection, critique, and calls for accountability for leaders, security services, and other political players. In contrast, instead of using the grim third anniversary of October 7 to learn and evolve, significant elements of the “pro-Palestine” industrial complex remain one of the most embarrassing and backward hate-driven movements in contemporary political activism.

This is not a real pro-Palestine movement. It is a virulent anti-Israel bloc built on ignorance, mob mentality, open sympathy for terrorism, and sabotage of the Palestinian people’s legitimate pursuit of freedom and prosperity. Its regressive and poisonous rhetoric will not evolve into anything constructive. It should be treated with contempt, stripped of relevance, and isolated until it collapses and makes room for a serious effort that actually cares about Palestinians rather than the fantasies of wannabe revolutionaries.

text:
Today marks another year since the horrific terrorist attacks of October 7, 2023, a day of unimaginable loss that forever changed the lives of so many families in Israel and around the world.

A month and a half ago, I traveled to Israel, and had the profound opportunity to sit down with survivors and hear their stories firsthand. I listened as they shared what they endured, the loved ones they lost, and how they have found the strength to say they want peace.

Their stories have stayed with me.

I made this documentary because these voices deserve to be heard and remembered. At a moment when the pain of October 7 can too easily become reduced to headlines, arguments, and statistics, I wanted people to hear directly from those who lived through it, to see their humanity, their grief, and their resilience.

On this anniversary, I am remembering the lives that were taken, standing with the survivors and families who continue to carry this trauma, and recommitting myself to the work of combating terrorism, antisemitism and pursuing a future where Israelis and Palestinians can live with safety, dignity, and lasting peace.

I hope you’ll take a few minutes to watch and hear their stories.

I'm a person of faith, and that faith matters deeply to me. So does the promise our framers made in the First Amendment, that no American, whatever they believe or don't believe, should ever have a government that serves one set of religious beliefs instead of serving the people.

The Establishment Clause is the very first protection in our Bill of Rights. 

Thomas Jefferson described it as building a "wall of separation between church and state," and for more than two centuries that wall has kept faith free to flourish on its own terms.

Few people depend on that promise more than our servicemembers, who come from every faith tradition and from none, and who all swear the same oath to the same Constitution. Secretary Pete Hegseth seems to have lost sight of that.  

Keeping government out of religion protects every American's freedom to worship as they choose, including his own.

The Constitution draws a clear line here. 

Those of us who cherish both our faith and our Constitution have a duty to stand up and say the Pentagon must never become a pulpit.

text:
My Administration continues to move aggressively to fix the serious system error at the Motor Vehicle Commission left behind by the previous administration to ensure our elections remain free, fair, and secure. I promised we would be thorough to ensure that no one who is ineligible remains on the voter rolls, and that every eligible voter has their voice heard. 

Leaving no stone unturned, I directed my Administration to conduct a thorough review of all voter-registration processes at the MVC and implement reforms to strengthen those processes.

This review surfaced two issues. Neither issue involved noncitizens.

The review identified approximately 750 additional records affected by the IDEMIA system error from June 2023 to June 2024 that require further action. These individuals selected “no” on the age-eligibility prompt, but their records were sent through for registration. These individuals’ dates of birth confirm they were old enough to vote, and no underage person voted as a result of this error. They appear to have pressed the wrong button on the PIN pad by mistake.  

Additionally, the review identified approximately 340 potentially improper voter-registration records from the MVC re-entry events dating back to 2016.  

The review showed that this issue had gone undetected and unaddressed, with some going as far back as a decade. My Administration found them and moved immediately to fix them.

text:
I directed the MVC to take the necessary steps to strengthen our registration processes and enact stronger safeguards. In addition to transitioning to a new vendor, the MVC is in the process of implementing agency-wide reforms, with many already completed, that add new layers of review and quality control to the voter-registration process. These include:  
- Deploying an automated audit process that verifies voter-registration records against customers’ recorded responses at the end of each day before being transmitted to DOE.  
- Creating an escalation and remediation plan so that any anomaly flagged by the daily audit is reported to MVC leadership and tracked through investigation and correction.  
- Adding clear signage in MVC Mobile Units for Department of Corrections (DOC) re-entry events to ensure individuals understand voter-eligibility requirements.   
- Making the registration process clearer and more accessible, through expanded language and translation assistance and clearer explanations of voter-eligibility requirements.  
- Developing a PIN pad prompt at re-entry events where individuals seeking to register must confirm they are not currently incarcerated for an indictable offense, to prevent similar errors found in our review.

This day is profoundly painful for so many New Yorkers. It marks three years since the horrific war crimes of October 7. On that day, Hamas killed more than 1,100 Israelis and abducted 251 others. We grieve alongside our many friends and neighbors who still carry that unthinkable loss.

The suffering did not begin nor end that day. It instead continued through the Israeli government’s devastating, ongoing genocide in Gaza, in which it has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians—including more than 21,000 children. Even since the so-called ceasefire, more than 1,400 Palestinians have been killed. That suffering has intensified with every Israeli bomb dropped on ambulances waiting outside hospitals, every drone strike targeting a residential building or journalist, and every shipment of food aid turned away at a border crossing. Many New Yorkers are reckoning with this unbearable grief, and we mourn alongside them – all while knowing that our tax dollars fund these war crimes.

Three years later, we must refuse to accept a world in which occupation and apartheid continue, where war crimes are met with impunity, and our federal government continues its complicity with every arms shipment.

To honor the dead, we must fight for a world in which every person can live with freedom, safety, and dignity.

You can scream fraud until you’re blue in the face, but if someone accused of it waves a check in front of you and suddenly gets a pass, then you don’t actually give a damn about fighting fraud.

And that’s exactly what Trump and his DOJ did with Guatam Adani, one of the richest people in the world.

The Biden Justice Department indicted him for a $265 million scheme to bribe Indian government officials and defraud American investors.

Then Trump took office. Adani’s lawyer, Robert Giuffra, who also happens to be one of Donald Trump's personal attorneys, walked into the Justice Department with an offer: drop the charges, and Adani will invest $10 billion in the U.S. economy.

And guess what? The charges were dropped.

This is NOT what justice is supposed to look like, and you don’t have to be a lawyer to know that.

When this Administration talks about fighting fraud, what they mean is fighting fraud that doesn’t come with a check attached. This is the most corrupt administration in American history, and they are not even trying to hide it.
https://t.co/c6gnRxEONv

May we remember the lives taken and families shattered three years ago today. And recommit ourselves, every day, to a world that affirms the dignity of Israelis and Palestinians alike.

text:
Every American, regardless of party, should be able to agree that if you are a U.S. citizen, the government should not be able to handcuff you, hold you without a lawyer, or deport you because of how you look or sound.

Yet there are now more than 500 documented cases of American citizens detained by immigration agents since last year. 

More than 70 were children. 

Around a dozen citizens, mostly kids, were deported. 

One man in Texas told officers he was a citizen. Four days later he was deported to Mexico. 

A Trump voter in North Carolina was pulled from his truck and pinned to the pavement even after proving his citizenship. 

His daughter now carries her passport to college.

The Constitution protects all of us, and when those protections erode for some, they erode for everyone.

We must secure our border while still treating people with basic dignity. 

That's exactly what our bipartisan Dignity Act does. It invests in border security, gives long-settled immigrants a tough but fair path to earn legal status, and frees enforcement to focus on real threats. I won’t stop until we get it done.
https://t.co/g7jRQ80LkY

text:
Late last month, I met with Iraqi Foreign Minister Fuad Hussein and Iraq’s new Ambassador to the U.S., Krikor Der Hagopian, coincidentally on the day that the last U.S. forces, after many years, finally pulled out of Iraq.

The moment was a little surreal for me, as I did three tours in Iraq alongside the military.  After decades of dwindling American military involvement, Iraq now has the opportunity to write its next chapter with Iraqis fully responsible for their country’s security.

That transition will not always be easy. Iraq’s long-term stability depends on the government, not armed militias, controlling its territory and decisions of war and peace. The ongoing U.S.-Iran conflict makes that challenge even harder, as we discussed in our meeting. Many of us will be watching closely as the Iraqi government continues its work to disarm these groups and build a more stable and prosperous Iraq.

Michigan is home to the largest Iraqi-American community in the country, so what happens in Iraq reverberates in Michigan. That is why our conversation also included advocating for the safety of Iraqis who have been deported from the U.S., dual citizens in detention, and the rights of minorities groups, including the Chaldean community.

South Texas students have the talent to compete for some of the most advanced science and technology jobs in the country.

In the FY26 Energy and Water Development Appropriations bill, I helped secure $25 million for the National Nuclear Security Administration’s Minority Serving Institution Partnership Program.

The program connects students at Hispanic-Serving and other Minority-Serving Institutions with research, internships, and hands-on opportunities at our national laboratories and other NNSA facilities. These partnerships help students build experience in fields like engineering, cybersecurity, advanced manufacturing, and nuclear security while preparing them for careers that are important to our national security. 

As a senior member of the House Appropriations Committee, I will continue working to expand opportunities for South Texas students and strengthen the pipeline from our classrooms to good-paying STEM careers.
